newsitem.title: USA: U.S. state faces growing pressure to halt execution.
newsitem.headline: U.S. state faces growing pressure to halt execution.

text.p: The state of Virginia is facing growing international pressure including a call from the pope to stop the planned execution of a man who says he has DNA evidence proving his innocence.

The case of Joseph O'Dell, scheduled to die by lethal injection on Wednesday, has sparked street protests in Rome, visits by Sister Helen Prejean, the author of "Dead Man Walking," and a plea for clemency straight from the Vatican.
Virginia has already executed a record seven people this year and was preparing to put another to death on Monday with the scheduled execution of Ronald Lee Hoke Jr., a convicted rapist and murderer.

O'Dell's case, however, has drawn intense fire from death penalty opponents at home and abroad who are demanding Virginia halt Wednesday's execution in order to consider new evidence the 55-year-old convict says will set him free.

O'Dell, who represented himself at his 1985 trial, was convicted of raping and murdering Helen Schartner of Virginia Beach, Virginia, a secretary whom he allegedly abducted at gunpoint. Now he says new DNA evidence emerged three years after the trial that proves blood found on a shirt and jacket he wore did not match that of the victim.

"The main evidence at trial, the evidence that I think the jury relied on, was blood test evidence and that evidence has been completely undermined and contradicted by what's come along later on," O'Dell's lawyer Robert Smith told CNN.

O'Dell said the blood got on his clothes when he broke up a fight. Armed with the DNA test, he appealed his death sentence, but court officials refused to admit the finding into evidence on the grounds that the blood sample was too degraded to be conclusive.

With just two days to go before the scheduled execution, O'Dell's supporters are pressing even harder on Virginia Gov. George Allen, who says he will not consider acting until the U.S. Supreme Court decides whether it will hear O'Dell's petition for a stay.
The Supreme Court tends to avoid hearing death penalty appeals and Allen has granted clemency only once.

O'Dell has been visited twice by Sister Prejean, the nun whose book "Dead Man Walking" was made into a powerful movie this year, and one of the original investigators in his case believed him strongly enough to marry him on death row.
"Evidence in this case reveals a gross miscarriage of justice that was perpetrated by the state of Virginia," his wife, Lori Urs, said.

O'Dell's bid to escape the deadly injection also won the backing of Pope John Paul II, who last week directed the Vatican's representative in Washington to intercede in his name to try to save the condemned man.

"You don't count on that kind of support but it's the kind of case where there has to be very real concerns about what's right here," O'Dell's lawyer told CNN. "(The pope) believes as we do that it would be a horribly wrong thing for this man to be executed," Smith said.

Last week in Italy, which has no death penalty, about 50 protesters demonstrated outside the U.S. Embassy in Rome and on Friday officials said they had conveyed concern over O'Dell's fate to the U.S. government.

O'Dell's case has not so far drawn much publicity in the United States, where 38 states have the death penalty. Texas leads the nation with 107 executions since capital punishment was reinstated in 1976, followed by Florida with 38.
